Mezzo-soprano. Mezzo-soprano, literally half-soprano in Italian, is the female voice type between soprano and alto, commanding a warm, robust middle-to-lower range ideal for heroic and character roles. Though ranked as secondary to the soprano in Classical opera hierarchies, mezzo-sopranos have created some of opera's most memorable performances as witches, warriors, seductresses, and complex protagonists. The voice type rose in prestige through the nineteenth and twentieth centuries as composers recognized its unique dramatic power. The mezzo-soprano range typically spans from around A3 to E6, lying lower than soprano but higher than alto. Naturally produced chest resonance gives mezzo-sopranos a distinctive warm, penetrating timbre suited to dramatic intensity. Mezzo roles in Classical opera were often secondary, like nurses and confidantes, but the Romantic era elevated them to leads. Carmen in Bizet's Carmen remains the iconic mezzo role—a free-spirited, dangerous woman whose low range carries seductive power. The Habanera, Carmen's most famous aria, sits in the mezzo's sweet spot and requires both lyrical beauty and fierce personality. Composers from Rossini to Verdi to Wagner wrote substantial mezzo roles, particularly for male-to-female vocal dynamics and dramatic variety. Modern opera houses feature prominent mezzo-sopranos performing roles traditionally sung by both female and male singers, including trouser roles.
